Backfill for streaming behavioral cohorts
## Problem The streaming cohorts pipeline (`cohort-event-shuffler` + `cohort-stream-processor`) computes membership only from events it sees live. It has no memory of anything that happened before it started watching. Five real situations depend on history it can never observe live: | # | Trigger | What is missing | |---|---------|-----------------| | T1 | Team enabled (allowlist flip) | All windowed state for that team's cohorts | | T2 | New cohort created | State for all history inside the cohort's window | | T3 | Cohort edited (window, threshold, filter) | State under the new key; old members stay members forever (a confirmed cutover blocker) | | T4 | Store loss or schema bump (e.g. the v3 wipe) | Everything since `now - max(window)` | | T5 | Dormant persons | Person property state for people who never emit events | None of this is built today. The flag serving gate `Cohort.is_flag_compatible` already requires `last_backfill_events_at` to be set for a behavioral cohort, but nothing in production writes that column, so the gate stays permanently closed. ## Core idea We compute the historical state with the exact same evaluator the live processor uses, aggregate it into small mergeable tiles, and feed those tiles into the processor through a new topic. state.ticket:
Object-level access controls for llm_prompt can be created but are never enforced

incremental sync skips records with null updated_at
The Chargebee source attaches the incremental cursor param `updated_at[after]` to every request when a schema uses the incremental sync method, including the first sync, where the cursor is the initial value 0 (`incremental_param()` in `products/warehouse_sources/backend/temporal/data_imports/sources/chargebee/chargebee.py`). Chargebee applies that filter server-side, and records with no `updated_at` attribute are excluded from the response. Per [Chargebee's API docs]( `updated_at` "will be present only if the resource has been updated after 2016-09-28", and in practice some records never receive one at all (observed on voided authorization transactions created in 2020-2022). Those records can never be imported while the schema is incremental, and a full resync doesn't help because the filter is still sent. The gap is silent: jobs report Completed and the table looks healthy. Verified on a customer site: a direct unfiltered `GET /api/v2/transactions` export contained 7,836 unique transactions while the warehouse table had 7,400, and the 436-record diff classified exactly as the records with null `updated_at` (every record with a populated `updated_at` was present). Switching the schema to full refresh omits the param and imports the missing records, which is the workaround for now. Support iOS release metadata from Info.plist in posthog-cli
## Problem The iOS and React Native upload wrappers now need the same release metadata that the SDK reports from `Bundle.main.infoDictionary`: - [PostHog/posthog-ios#776]( resolves it for native dSYM uploads. - [PostHog/posthog-js#4602]( resolves it for Hermes source maps. Both wrappers read `CFBundleShortVersionString` and `CFBundleVersion` from `INFOPLIST_FILE`, resolve simple Xcode build-setting references from the environment, and fall back to `MARKETING_VERSION` and `CURRENT_PROJECT_VERSION`. Keeping separate shell implementations risks attribution differences between native symbols and source maps. ## Proposed change Add an `--info-plist <path>` option to the posthog-cli release arguments used by `dsym upload` and Hermes source-map commands. The CLI should: - read the bundle identifier, short version, and build number from the plist; - resolve exact Xcode build-setting references such as `$(APP_VERSION)` and `${BUILD_NUMBER}` from the environment; - let explicit `--release-name`, `--release-version`, and `--build` arguments take precedence; - return no value for unresolved or compound substitutions so callers can retain their existing fallback behavior. This would let both upload wrappers pass the plist path instead of maintaining duplicate release-resolution logic.

state.ticket:
Decide the repair contract for membership transitions lost between state commit and produce
The cohort stream processor commits evaluation state to RocksDB first, then produces the resulting membership transitions to Kafka, and advances consumer offsets only after the produce succeeds. A produce failure holds the offset so the event replays, but the replay evaluates against the already committed state, sees no flip, and never emits the transition again. A crash between the state commit and the produce loses the transition the same way. Two sweep code paths additionally drop their output on produce failure on purpose (`rust/cohort-stream-processor/src/workers/worker.rs`). That was acceptable while the output was a shadow topic nobody consumed. It is not acceptable once the CDP consumer writes the transitions to Postgres, because a lost transition leaves the table permanently wrong with no signal. Pick one of two fixes before the cutover. Either produce before committing state so a replay emits the transition again, accepting duplicate messages since the consumer upsert is idempotent, or bless scheduled periodic reconcile snapshots as the healing mechanism, with a named owner and a cadence.

state.ticket:
Build mark and sweep deletion in the CDP cohort membership consumer
When a cohort definition is edited, a reconcile run replays the cohort's full current membership as a snapshot tagged with a run id, then emits one completion marker per processor partition on the dedicated `cohort_reconcile_markers` topic. The CDP membership consumer today only upserts (`nodejs/src/cdp/consumers/cdp-cohort-membership.consumer.ts`). Live transitions flip `in_cohort`, but a person who no longer matches an edited definition gets no live transition and no snapshot message, so their row stays `in_cohort = true` in the `cohort_membership` Postgres table forever. The designed fix is mark and sweep: once every completion marker for a run has arrived, remove the rows for that cohort whose version is older than the run. This was designed but never built or exercised. Building it needs four pieces: parse the `run_id` field the processor already emits instead of discarding it, add a version column to the `cohort_membership` table, consume the marker topic, and run the sweep once all markers for a run have arrived.

state.ticket:
Make cohort processor disaster recovery real before downstream depends on membership state
All membership evaluation state lives in RocksDB on a single pod's local volume. Losing that volume today means rerunning backfills, which is annoying but harmless because nothing consumes the output yet. Once the `cohort_membership` Postgres table feeds workflows or feature flags, a lost volume becomes a long outage while state rebuilds. The processor has an S3 checkpoint and restore layer, but it is off by default (`CHECKPOINT_ENABLED` in `rust/cohort-stream-processor/src/config.rs`), has never run in production, and no bucket or access role is provisioned. Known defects to fix before enabling it. There is no periodic full upload, so a checkpoint can reference arbitrarily old files and a bucket retention policy would delete files a restore still needs, silently breaking recovery. A failed restore logs a warning and cold starts with an empty store instead of alerting. Enabling checkpoints without configuring a bucket silently does nothing. There is no metric for bytes uploaded, so cost cannot be sized. Fix the defects, provision the bucket and access, then run a restore drill and verify that a pod restored from S3 serves correct membership.

warn when uploaded symbol sets are never matched
## Is your feature request related to a problem? When source map upload is configured but the built bundle is not stamped with chunk IDs, nothing in PostHog says so. Symbol sets upload successfully, they appear in the project settings list, `has_uploaded_file` is true, and no `failure_reason` is set. Meanwhile every incoming stack frame stays minified, because no frame carries a chunk ID to match a symbol set against. PostHog already knows this is happening, and writes `resolve_failure: "No chunk id sent with frame"` onto the frames. ## Is your feature request related to a problem? A customer backfilled a person property (acquisition_channel) onto their customer base via warehouse person properties and wants to break down a running experiment's funnel metric by it. The values never show up: experiment breakdowns evaluate person properties at event time, and the backfill only updates the person, not the person_properties snapshot on historical events. A ticket created from the SDK or the API lands on the widget channel, and replies on a widget ticket are only readable inside the widget. Teams that want to own their intake UI, whether that is a contact form on a marketing site or a custom in-app help page, can create the ticket but have no way to get the answer back to the person who wrote in. alerts that can pause or stop an experiment
### Feature request ## Is your feature request related to a problem? Customer research asked for this directly: if a metric moves too much while an experiment is running, they want to be able to shut the experiment down. Today nothing watches a running experiment's metrics, and there is no path from "a metric moved badly" to "the experiment stops serving". Someone must see the movement, open the experiment, and stop it by hand. Two pieces are needed: 1. **Alerts on experiment metrics** — a watch on a primary or guardrail metric that fires when the movement crosses a threshold or an anomaly detector. 2. **Action on metric movement** — a response the user configures in advance, including pausing or stopping the experiment (and so the underlying feature flag rollout). Mark a ticket as unread after reading it
## Is your feature request related to a problem? - An agent opens a ticket, reads it, and cannot put it back in the unread state. - Opening a ticket clears the team unread counter, and nothing sets it again. - Agents use unread as a personal to-do marker. - When that marker clears by accident, the ticket drops out of view and the reply waits longer than it should. - Retrieving a ticket sets `unread_team_count` to 0 (`products/conversations/backend/api/tickets.py:1056`). No endpoint reverses this. ## Describe the solution you'd like - Add a "Mark as unread" action on the ticket page and in the inbox row menu. - Restore the unread state for the team side only. Do not touch the customer counter. - Add the same action to the bulk actions on the ticket list, so an agent can mark several tickets at once. ## Describe alternatives you've considered - Make "Unread" a ticket status next to new, open, pending, on hold, and resolved. - This gives one field to reason about, and filtering comes for free. - Unread is a count per side today, team and customer. One status cannot hold both. - A status also competes with the workflow meaning, because a ticket can be open and unread at the same time. - Snooze a ticket. This is the nearest thing that exists, but it hides a ticket instead of raising it. ## Additional context - Internal support ticket 74594. - Pairs with the unread filter request, #104779.

Rename, delete, and merge ticket tags
## Is your feature request related to a problem? - Teams cannot manage their support tags. - There is no way to rename a tag, delete a tag, or move every ticket from one tag to another. - A typo in a tag name stays until the last ticket drops it, because cleanup only removes a tag after it has no tickets left. - The tag list grows messy, and a messy list makes the tag filter less useful. - The support product has no tag management endpoint and no settings page for tags. ## Describe the solution you'd like - Add a tag page in support settings that lists each tag with its ticket count. - From that page, let an agent: - Rename a tag. This covers the tagA to tagB conversion. - Write each action to the activity log, because one action changes many tickets. ## Describe alternatives you've considered - Bulk tag editing on the ticket list, which exists already (#74760). - An agent can filter by tagA, select the tickets, add tagB, then remove tagA. - This works on a small tag. ### Feature request ## Is your feature request related to a problem? When building dashboards for stakeholders, the current funnel visualization options (horizontal/vertical bar charts, historical trends, and time-to-convert histogram) don't convey the "funnel" concept visually. ## Is your feature request related to a problem? Customer hitting an API rate limit for a prompt. Currently polling prompts on a 5min fixed interval. Have multiple backends polling. ## Describe the solution you'd like Prompt fetches could behave more like feature flag evaluation: 1. One endpoint that returns all the prompts a client needs in one request (see #95460 for the label-aware collection fetch). 2. A rate limit for prompt reads that is separate from the general API limit and sized for many polling clients, like the flag definitions endpoint. 3. Cacheable responses. Prompts do not have to be real time. Data that is a few minutes old is acceptable, so a CDN or HTTP cache layer (for example `Cache-Control` with a short max-age, or ETags so that an unchanged poll is cheap) is a good fit. ## Describe alternatives you've considered - A customer-hosted shared cache or proxy. It works, but it adds infrastructure and a failure point. - Longer SDK cache TTLs. They lower the rate per process, but the total still scales with the process count. ## Additional context Top priority from customer feedback. Related: #95460 (fetch all prompts at a label in one request), PostHog/posthog-js#4353 (SDK batch fetch).

state.ticket:
prompt variables in the playground
## Is your feature request related to a problem? Teams compose long prompts in source code and interpolate variables at runtime. The prompt page shows variables, which is useful at a glance for long prompts, but users cannot do much with them in the UI. To test a prompt with real values, they must copy it out and fill the variables by hand. ## Describe the solution you'd like 1. In the playground, let users enter a value for each variable in the prompt and run the prompt with those values. 2. Optionally, save sets of variable values as test inputs, so that users can run the same inputs again after they edit the prompt. 3. Make variables more useful on the prompt page, for example a list of variables with where each one is used. We currently show a list of all variables used in a per-prompt view. ## Describe alternatives you've considered Interpolation in application code only. This works at runtime, but gives no way to test in PostHog. ## Additional context From customer feedback on prompt management.

state.ticket:
global prompt change history
## Is your feature request related to a problem? When a production issue happens, teams want to know if a prompt change caused it. Today they must open each prompt to see its version history. There is no single view of all prompt changes across the project. ## Describe the solution you'd like A global prompt history: one activity feed for all prompts in the project, with who changed which prompt, when, and what changed (new version, label moved, prompt archived). `LLMPrompt` and `LLMPromptLabel` are already activity-logged scopes, so this can build on the existing activity log. Useful additions: - Filter by prompt, by label (for example only `production` label changes), and by time range. - Show prompt changes as annotations on LLM analytics charts, so a change lines up with a metric shift. ## Describe alternatives you've considered The per-prompt version history. It does not help when you do not know which prompt changed. ## Additional context From customer feedback on prompt management.

state.ticket:
prompt usage data when prompts are fetched in bulk
## Is your feature request related to a problem? Teams that fetch all their prompts in bulk get no useful usage data. The data shows that all prompts were fetched, but not which prompts the application actually uses, or how often. To connect prompts to generations, teams must set up tracing and link prompts in the SDK by hand, which takes manual work. ## Describe the solution you'd like 1. Show prompt usage from traces: which generations used which prompt and version. Make it clear on the prompt page when no trace data is linked, and show how to fix this. 2. Make the prompt-to-trace link as close to automatic as possible in the SDKs, for example when a prompt that the SDK fetched is passed to a traced LLM call. 3. Let the self-driving setup (the wizard) add tracing and prompt linking to a codebase, so that teams do not have to do the integration work by hand. ## Describe alternatives you've considered Fetch counts per prompt. They are not accurate for bulk fetches, and they do not show real usage. ## Additional context From customer feedback on prompt management. Related: #61811 (prompt name and version dropped on OTel ingestion, which also breaks the prompt-to-trace link).

state.ticket:
live scoring of production responses for prompts
## Is your feature request related to a problem? Some teams have no prompt testing and no A/B testing of prompts in production. Evals are run by a separate research team, on scored prompt sets, apart from production releases. Production responses are not scored, so offline evals are the only feedback loop. ## Describe the solution you'd like This is an idea to explore: 1. Continuous live scoring of production responses (online evaluations on a sample of generations), per prompt and version. 2. Send low-scoring or interesting production cases back to datasets that the offline eval sets use, so production results feed into research work. 3. Prompt experiments: serve two prompt versions to different users through a feature flag, and compare quality, cost, and outcome metrics. ## Describe alternatives you've considered Offline evals only. They do not show how a prompt performs on real traffic. ## Additional context Idea from customer feedback on prompt management.

Filter rules per support ticket channel
## Is your feature request related to a problem? Every inbound item on a connected support channel becomes a ticket. There is no way to tell a channel to ignore some of them. On the GitHub channel this fills the inbox with activity that is not support work. Pull requests and issues opened by our own team or by bots all arrive as tickets. A rule says which inbound items the channel must ignore. The ignored items must not reach the inbox or the ticket counts. ## Describe alternatives you've considered - Close the unwanted tickets by hand. This works, but it costs time every day. - Turn off the GitHub channel. This also stops the tickets we want. - Use a workflow to close the tickets after creation. The tickets still appear in the inbox and in the counts. ## Additional context The same rule model is useful on the other channels. One example is to ignore email from a known automated sender. Raised from support ticket 76716.

state.ticket:
custom metadata on tickets, readable and writable from workflows
## Is your feature request related to a problem? A ticket only holds the fields conversations defines: status, priority, tags, assignee, SLA. A workflow has nowhere to keep its own data about a ticket. That blocks a useful pattern. I want every ticket to get a Slack thread, so the team can follow it in Slack even when the ticket arrives by email. A workflow can post the first Slack message, but it can't store the thread ID that comes back. The next run can't find that thread, so it posts a new message instead of a reply. The thread never becomes a running status update. Any other external ID hits the same wall: a Linear issue key, an incident ID, a vendor case number. ## Describe the solution you'd like Somewhere on the ticket to store arbitrary key-value data that workflows can read and write. In practice that means a metadata input on "Update ticket", metadata returned by "Get ticket", and the same field on the ticket API. Seeing those keys on the ticket itself would also help, so a support agent can tell why a ticket links to an external thread. ## Describe alternatives you've considered Tags are the closest thing today, but a tag is a label a person picks from a list. Thread IDs would pollute tag autocomplete. Keeping the mapping in an external store works, but it means running a service outside PostHog for data that belongs on the ticket. ## Additional context Related: #89852, #104780, #104781, #60282. state.ticket:

Tracks the build of rollback suggestions for feature flags: when an edit that increases a flag's exposure is followed by a rise in errors attributable to it, PostHog tells the person who made the edit and the flag's creator, and offers a revert they apply with one click. Design: PostHog/requests-for-comments-internal#1298 (internal). Related feature request: #22883. ## How it works - Every edit that increases a flag's exposure opens an observation window. Windows only open when the project has the scout on, the organization approved AI data processing, no other product owns the flag, and the flag isn't opted out. - A scheduled Temporal workflow in the flags product scores open windows with HogQL, one query per team, without an LLM. - A suspicious window triggers a Signals scout. It goes through the regular flag update, so approval policies still apply. - A flags overview page lists the flag reports that need attention and the recently launched flags with the state of their window. - The revert is never automatic. ## Phases Each item is one small PR, unless it's marked as a task. `cohort-stream-processor` runs as one pod per region, and that pod holds the state of all 64 partitions. This issue tracks running it as N pods, each owning 64/N partitions. Restarts, failures and reshards must lose no membership and must never certify wrong membership. GA depends on it. Capacity does not force this yet. state.ticket:
stop catalog races from stranding backfill runs
Part of #114193. Each processor pod refreshes its cohort catalog on its own timer, every 300 s with up to 60 s of jitter. A reconcile job pins a shape hash. When the pod's catalog does not have that hash yet, the guard discards the job as `hash_unknown` or `hash_mismatch` (`evaluate_guard` in `rust/cohort-stream-processor/src/workers/reconcile.rs`). The discard commits the seed offset and sends nothing. The seeder then records a retryable shortfall, and nothing re-dispatches it, so the run stays in `reconciling` until someone intervenes. Automatic dispatch only heals runs whose reconcile was never dispatched. A manual re-dispatch resets every participation and sends tiles to all 64 partitions. This already happens at one pod when a run starts right after its cohorts' shape hashes are written. With N pods refreshing at different times, it happens more often. **Action** 1. In the processor, retry an unknown or mismatched hash until one catalog refresh after the job arrived, then discard. This is per pod and needs no seeder change, so do it first. 2. Send discards as the outcome marker from #114194, and have the seeder settle them. A re-dispatch must skip partitions withheld as cold, or it discards again. 3. Alert on discards while a run of that kind is active. **Done when** a person-property run created right after its cohorts' shape hashes are written completes with no operator step. **Depends on** #114194 for step 2. Step 1 can start now.

state.ticket:
stop the seeder running twice during a rollout
Part of #114193. The seeder runs as one replica, but its rolling update starts the new pod before it stops the old one, so every rollout briefly runs two seeders. The ledger is safe with two replicas. Claims use `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, and every write checks the claim epoch. The budgets are not safe. Slots, pacers, the circuit breaker and planning backoff are all per process, so two seeders double ClickHouse concurrency and the seed rate. One replica's breaker can also fail a run that the other is still advancing. `docs/internal/realtime-cohorts/seeder.md` describes the seeder as "a set of replicas", which does not match how it runs. **Action** - Switch the seeder's deployment to the `Recreate` strategy until its budgets are shared across replicas. - Make the doc say the seeder runs as a singleton, and why. **Done when** a seeder rollout never runs two pods at once. **Depends on** nothing.

state.ticket:
repair a backfill that falls short without an operator
A backfill run reconciles each of its cohorts and records an outcome for each one. When an outcome is missing and the error is retryable, nothing repairs the run without an operator. **Today** - The Django finalizer holds the run in `reconciling` and treats the shortfall as one that "simply holds until re-dispatch" (`products/cohorts/backend/backfill/finalize.py`). - The seeder's auto-dispatch re-dispatches only runs with no usable dispatch record (`rust/cohort-seeder/src/app/completion.rs`). - Completion discovery skips runs that already carry `reconcile_observed_at` (`rust/cohort-seeder/src/store/completion.rs`). - So the run waits for an operator to run `reconcile_dispatch`. Its cohorts stay unready, and only a stall alert hours later shows it. **Action** 1. Re-dispatch a held run on its own, with backoff and a cap on attempts. 2. When the cap is reached, fail the run so a new one can replace it. 3. Count held runs, re-dispatches and failures by reason. **Done when** a run held on a retryable shortfall completes or fails with no operator step, and a test covers both paths.

state.ticket:
keep processor state proportional to enabled cohorts
One processor pod keeps the state of every enabled team today. A rollout to every team needs that state to be small, and to grow with what cohorts read rather than with what a team sends. Multi-pod in #114193 spreads the state, but it does not make it smaller. **Today** - The eviction queue is on the heap and holds every behavioral key twice: a `BTreeMap` by deadline and a `HashMap` reverse index (`rust/cohort-stream-processor/src/sweep/eviction_queue.rs`). Memory grows with the number of keys, and every restart rebuilds the queue. - Each state row carries replay marks, a map from source partition to offset (`AppliedOffsets` in `rust/cohort-stream-processor/src/stage1/state.rs`). Nothing prunes the map. - On a team with a person-property condition, the processor keeps a record for every person it sees, whether or not anything reads the cohort. - State values are JSON. **Action** 1. Measure bytes per person and memory per key on a production-shaped team. 2. Move the eviction index off the heap. 3. Bound the replay marks. 4. Use a compact encoding for state values. 5. Keep state only for enabled cohorts, after #120357. **Done when** memory per key and bytes per person are measured, and a team's state grows with its enabled cohorts, not with its event volume.

state.ticket:
no-code web experiment changes show up on pages you didn't pick them on The toolbar's element picker finds a selector that's unique on the page you're standing on. Web experiments then apply it on every page. So if you pick an element that comes from a shared component, your variant changes it everywhere that component renders. It's worst on sites with generated class names. The `wordLike` check in `frontend/src/toolbar/vendor/finder/index.ts` only accepts `/^[a-z-]{3,}$/i`, which rejects a class like `Checkout-module-scss-module__a1b2c3__title` and an id like `__next`. With nothing left to use, the picker falls back to the bare tag and saves `h1` as the selector for a site-wide heading. ## How to reproduce 1. Serve two pages that share a heading component, where the heading's only class is a generated one: ```html

Buy now

Welcome

``` 2. Open `/product` with the toolbar, create a web experiment, and pick the heading. The saved selector is `h1`. 3. Launch it, then load `/` as a user who gets the test variant. 4. The heading on `/` changed too. ## Additional context I tried this with CSS modules, styled-components, Tailwind, and plain semantic class names. All four leaked. Only an `id` or a configured `data-attr` on the element itself gave a page-scoped selector.

## Is your feature request related to a problem? A flag can depend on another flag that isn't evaluated in the same runtime. For example, a server flag can depend on a client-only flag. [`_validate_flag_reference`]( checks that a dependency exists, is active, and uses a supported format, but it doesn't look at `evaluation_runtime`. state.ticket:
metric definitions as code for warehouse-native metrics
## Is your feature request related to a problem? Warehouse-native experiment metrics are built on data warehouse tables. Today, these metrics are created and changed in the PostHog app, or through the API. Teams with a data warehouse often keep their data definitions in files in a git repository. They want to keep their experiment metric definitions there too. This gives them: - A review step before a metric changes. - A history of who changed a metric, and when. - One trusted definition of each metric, stored next to their other data definitions. ## Describe the solution you'd like A way to define warehouse-native experiment metrics in files (for example YAML) and sync them to PostHog. A possible flow: 1. A team writes metric definitions in files in their repository. 2. When a change is merged, an automated job sends the files to PostHog. 3. PostHog creates or updates the matching warehouse-native metrics. 4. Metrics that come from files are marked in the app, and cannot be edited there. The files are the only place to change them. It would also help to export existing warehouse-native metrics to files, so teams do not have to start from zero. ## Describe alternatives you've considered Teams can write their own script that calls the API. This works, but each team has to build and maintain it, and the metrics can still be edited in the app. ## Additional context This request covers warehouse-native metrics only. Metrics built on PostHog events are not part of it.

state.ticket:
marketing analytics - choose which ad platform conversions are reported
## Is your feature request related to a problem? The "Reported conversions" column in Marketing analytics adds together every conversion type that PostHog maps for each ad platform, and users can't change which types are included. For Meta Ads, that means purchases, registrations, leads, subscribes and app installs are summed into one number. When an account sends a high-volume, low-value conversion (for example, a registration fired on account signup) alongside purchases, Reported conversions is several times higher than the purchase count in Meta Ads Manager. Cost per reported conversion and conversion rate use the same total, so they are off too. Users whose goal is purchases don't have a way to make Reported conversions show only purchases. ## Describe the solution you'd like Let users choose, per connected ad platform, which of that platform's conversion types count toward Reported conversions (and Reported conversion value), for example only `omni_purchase` for Meta Ads. ## Describe alternatives you've considered - Conversion goals: these count the user's own PostHog events (for example a purchase event), attributed by UTM. They're useful, but they are PostHog-attributed, not the numbers each ad platform reports, so they don't replace a platform-reported purchase count. - Querying the raw `actions` JSON in the synced `metaads` tables with SQL works, but it's outside Marketing analytics, and each platform needs its own query. ## Additional context From: Customer project

state.ticket:
mask the identity verification secret by default
## What happens On **Support → Settings → General**, the **Identity verification secret** field shows the full secret in plain text as soon as the page loads. You don't have to click "reveal". So anything that sees the page can read the secret: - a screen share - a screenshot - a browser automation or AI agent reading the page - someone looking over your shoulder You only need to open the settings to change something unrelated, such as a widget domain or the Slack channel. That is when it gets exposed. We hit this twice in one afternoon. Both times an assistant was changing unrelated Support settings for us. It read or screenshotted the page, the secret ended up in its transcript, and we had to rotate the secret each time. (The rotate + "Expire now" flow is good, thank you. It's just needed more often than it should be.) ## Suggestion - **Masking:** mask the secret by default (`••••••••abcd`, last 4 characters at most), with a reveal or copy button. - **Copying:** the copy button should copy the full value without showing it, as the Stripe and GitHub token pages do. - **Accessible text:** keep the full value out of the page's text and accessibility tree until it's revealed, so agents that read the DOM don't pick it up. - **Other secrets:** the same treatment may suit any other secret shown in project settings. ## Environment - PostHog Cloud EU - Support (Conversations) settings page, November 2026

state.ticket:
SDK local evaluation matches person_metadata cohort filters against the caller's created_at property
## Bug Description Since #62230, a cohort can filter on Person metadata > First seen (`type: "person_metadata"`, `key: "created_at"`). `/flags` reads that value from the persons table and ignores any `created_at` person property ([flag_matching_utils.rs#L547]( SDK local evaluation gets this wrong. The definitions endpoint sends the cohort filter unchanged ([local_evaluation.py#L770]( Most SDKs treat every filter type other than `cohort` and `flag` as a person property, so they match the filter against a `created_at` key in the person properties the caller passes. For a flag that targets such a cohort: - If the caller doesn't pass `created_at`, the SDK returns inconclusive and falls back to `/flags`. That's correct. - If the caller passes a `created_at` person property, the SDK returns a result based on that value instead of the person's real creation time, so it can disagree with `/flags`. #62230 mentions that some teams set their own `created_at` person property. ## How to reproduce With posthog-python at 933c3c7, create a flag whose only condition is a cohort with `{"type": "person_metadata", "key": "created_at", "operator": "is_date_after", "value": "2025-01-01"}` and evaluate it locally: - `person_properties={}` returns inconclusive. - `person_properties={"created_at": "2026-06-01"}` returns `True`. - `person_properties={"created_at": "2020-06-01"}` returns `False`. `/flags` returns the same answer in all three cases because it uses the person's actual `created_at`. ## Af

state.ticket:
error tracking - choose which exception properties show by default
## Is your feature request related to a problem? On an error tracking issue's Properties tab, the default table shows a fixed list of built-in properties plus a "Custom properties" section with the properties whose names don't start with `$`. Every other property is only visible after switching on the JSON toggle, which shows all properties on the event, unfiltered. To see a few specific `$` properties, or to read nested values such as job arguments or request params, users have to switch to the full JSON view and search through it. ## Describe the solution you'd like The requester suggested a single properties view that always renders values as rich JSON (nested values expandable), filtered by default to the same properties the table shows today, with the JSON toggle becoming a "Show all" option. They would also like to choose which properties show by default, per project. ## Describe alternatives you've considered - Switch on the JSON toggle and use the "Filter properties" box, which also filters the JSON view by property name. - Copy `$` properties to names without the `$` in SDK code (for example in a `before_send` callback) so they show under "Custom properties". The requester found this heavy, because the data is already on the event. - Add rows to the hardcoded built-in list, as #135312 (Rails job properties) and #136644 (request method, path, and user agent) did. This covers specific SDK properties, but a project cannot choose its own. ## Additional context From: Wher
